strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored NLP/speech problem: audio chaptering for long-form media. The framing is relevant, and the distinction between transcript-dependent and transcript-invariant evaluation is useful for the community.

The work is empirically broad. It compares text-based segmentation, hand-crafted acoustic feature augmentation, learned audio-only representations, and multimodal LLMs, and includes analyses by ASR quality, duration, speaker regime, and MLLM failure modes.

The proposed AudioSeg model gives a clear and substantial gain over the text-based MiniSeg variants under the paper's main T1 protocol, especially with Whisper Large features, supporting the claim that learned audio representations contain useful chaptering signals beyond sentence-level text.

The analysis of hand-crafted features is informative: pauses drive most of the gain, while speaker features matter more for multi-speaker recordings. This is a concrete, interpretable finding rather than only a leaderboard result.

The paper provides many implementation details in the appendix, including prompts, hyperparameters, feature extraction, alignment procedures, ASR WERs, and stratified results, which improves reproducibility.
weaknesses: The strongest claim, that transcript-free audio segmentation is superior to text-based approaches, is somewhat overstated. The best AudioSeg variant uses Whisper Large, an ASR-trained encoder likely encoding substantial lexical information, so it is not clear how much of the gain comes from acoustic cues versus implicit transcription-like representations.

Evaluation is formalized broadly, but the experiments mainly rely on T1. The paper introduces continuous-time T2 as the most direct formulation, yet does not report substantive T2 results, leaving part of the methodological contribution under-validated.

The study relies on a single English dataset with potentially noisy YouTube chapter annotations. This limits confidence that the conclusions generalize across domains, languages, annotation styles, or professional chaptering settings.

There is little evidence of statistical robustness: no confidence intervals, significance tests, or multi-seed variance are reported, despite several comparisons being modest in size and training potentially high-variance long-sequence models.

The fairness of comparisons could be improved. AudioSeg gets a strong pretrained speech encoder and a 6-second grid, while text systems depend on sentence segmentation, alignment, and MiniSeg-style architectures; stronger transcript-based long-context or timestamp-aware baselines might narrow the gap.

The evaluation protocol choices need more justification. Using default text-segmentation metric parameters on 6-second chunks because they match average sentence length is plausible but not fully validated, and boundary F1 on sparse chapter labels can be sensitive to tolerance/grid choices.

The MLLM section is useful but somewhat secondary and uneven: results are restricted to shorter videos, many outputs fail formatting or transcription quality, and the setup combines transcription, segmentation, and title generation while other systems are evaluated only for segmentation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and underexplored NLP/speech problem: automatic chaptering of long-form audio. The framing around transcript dependence, ASR-induced evaluation artifacts, and time-based evaluation is well motivated.

The empirical scope is reasonably broad: the paper compares text-only segmentation, text plus hand-crafted acoustic features, an audio-only architecture, several pretrained audio encoders, and multimodal LLM prompting/fine-tuning variants.

The proposed time-space evaluation protocols are a useful contribution. The distinction between reference-transcript, ASR-transcript, aligned-text, discrete-time, and continuous-time evaluation makes an important methodological point for this task.

The results support some sound findings: pauses help text-based segmentation, transcript quality measured by WER is not a simple predictor of chaptering performance, MLLMs currently struggle with long audio and instruction following, and Whisper-based audio representations are strong for this dataset.

The appendix provides useful implementation details, prompts, hyperparameters, feature extraction procedures, and additional stratified analyses, which improves reproducibility relative to many papers of this type.
weaknesses: The central claim that transcript-free audio chaptering is superior is overstated. The best audio-only model uses Whisper Large representations, which likely encode substantial linguistic information and may benefit from domain match with YouTube-style data; this is not strong evidence that acoustic information alone is generally superior to transcripts.

The evaluation contribution is only partially realized. The paper introduces continuous-time evaluation T2 but does not appear to use it in the main experiments, relying instead on 6-second discrete chunks and text-segmentation metrics whose parameter choices are only lightly justified.

The empirical evidence is limited to a single English dataset. Given that YTSeg is YouTube-derived and the strongest encoder may have relevant pretraining/domain overlap, generalization beyond this benchmark is uncertain.

Comparisons are not always clean. MLLM results are restricted to videos under 30 minutes, whereas other systems are evaluated more broadly; text-based models depend on forced alignment and sentence segmentation choices; and audio-only models operate at fixed 6-second windows. These differences complicate the broad ranking claims.

The paper lacks statistical uncertainty or significance testing. Several reported gains are modest, especially for hand-crafted features other than pauses, and the absence of confidence intervals makes it hard to judge robustness.

The analysis sometimes gives causal explanations that are plausible but not fully demonstrated, such as non-speech cues driving AudioSeg gains or ASR quality being weakly related to segmentation for reasons beyond WER. The DeepFilterNet ablation is suggestive but coarse.

The work evaluates segmentation boundaries but largely ignores chapter title quality, even though chaptering as a user-facing task includes meaningful titles. This narrows the practical contribution relative to the stated motivation.

Reproducibility is decent but incomplete: code and augmented data are promised rather than available in the manuscript, and key details such as data splits, model selection criteria, thresholding/calibration for boundary decisions, and computational cost for all models could be clearer.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored NLP/speech problem: chaptering long-form audio beyond transcript-only segmentation. The framing is relevant to computational linguistics, speech processing, and practical long-document navigation.

The evaluation-protocol discussion is a major strength. Distinguishing reference-transcript, ASR-transcript, aligned-text, discrete-time, and continuous-time protocols clarifies a real comparability problem in prior work, and the oracle/protocol analyses substantiate why transcript-invariant evaluation matters.

The experimental scope is broad and useful: text-only MiniSeg variants, text plus handcrafted acoustic features, an audio-only architecture with multiple pretrained encoders, and multimodal LLM baselines. This gives the paper more value as a systematic study than as just a model proposal.

The empirical results are convincing on the central claim that audio carries useful segmentation signal. Pauses improve text models substantially, audio-only models outperform text baselines with Whisper features, and DeepFilterNet ablations support the role of non-speech cues.

The paper is generally clear and reproducible in its high-level methodology: model architectures, features, prompts, hyperparameters, ASR variants, diarization categories, and evaluation settings are described in substantial detail, with code/data release promised.
weaknesses: The strongest claim that transcript-free segmentation is superior rests mainly on AudioSeg with Whisper Large representations. Since Whisper is trained for ASR and may encode substantial linguistic information, the result does not fully isolate audio/acoustic information from latent transcription-like information.

The study depends on a single English YouTube dataset. This is acknowledged, but it limits confidence that the conclusions generalize across domains, languages, annotation styles, and chaptering conventions.

The proposed AudioSeg architecture appears reasonable but not deeply analyzed. There are limited ablations of key architectural choices such as 6-second windows, local transformer depth, frozen versus tuned encoders, chunk length, or alternative pooling/decoding strategies.

The evaluation proposal is useful, but T1 still depends on an arbitrary discretization choice and default segmentation-metric parameters. Continuous-time T2 is formalized but not central in the reported experiments, leaving the most direct timestamp-based evaluation underused.

Some results would benefit from stronger statistical treatment. The paper reports many comparisons, but confidence intervals, significance tests, or variance over seeds are largely absent, which matters for modest gains such as some handcrafted feature improvements.

The MLLM experiments are interesting but somewhat uneven: they are restricted to shorter videos, affected by formatting/transcription failures, and use a small set of models and prompting/training setups. These results are informative but should be interpreted cautiously.

Reproducibility is good in description but not fully established at review time because code and AudioSeg are only promised for release, and the computational cost/data-processing pipeline for full replication may be substantial.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated and underexplored NLP/speech problem: long-form audio chaptering beyond transcript-only text segmentation. The framing is relevant to practical podcast/video/lecture navigation and fits ACL interests in spoken-language processing and multimodal NLP.

The evaluation-protocol discussion is a real contribution. Distinguishing reference-transcript, ASR-transcript, hybrid alignment, discrete-time, and continuous-time protocols clarifies a source of unfair comparison in prior work, and the oracle/protocol analyses support the claim that transcript-space evaluation can be lossy or inflated by transcript granularity.

The empirical study is broad and informative: it compares text-only MiniSeg variants, handcrafted acoustic features, learned audio encoders, MLLMs, different ASR qualities, duration regimes, speaker regimes, and a small out-of-domain AMI setting. The stratified analyses are especially useful for understanding where methods fail.

The central finding that audio representations can improve chaptering is supported by consistent results: pause features help text models, AudioSeg with Whisper Large substantially outperforms text baselines on YTSeg, and DeepFilterNet ablations provide some evidence that non-speech cues contribute.
Reproducibility is reasonably supported by architectural descriptions, feature definitions, prompts, hyperparameters, evaluation definitions, and stated release of AudioSeg/tooling and annotations.
weaknesses: The strongest claim, that transcript-free segmentation is superior and captures structure beyond transcripts, is somewhat overstated. The best AudioSeg uses Whisper Large, an ASR-pretrained model likely encoding substantial lexical/semantic information and trained on YouTube-like data; the comparison to MiniSeg with MiniLM-style sentence embeddings may conflate modality, encoder scale/pretraining, and domain match.

The evaluation design favors a 6-second discretization that is also AudioSeg's native prediction resolution. The authors examine other granularities and T2 collars, which helps, but the default T1 setup may still make boundary localization performance hard to interpret, especially relative to sentence-based systems projected through forced alignment.

Generalization evidence is limited. YTSeg dominates the study, while AMI evaluation is very small, especially the <30-minute condition with only 4 test meetings. The paper acknowledges this, but the breadth of conclusions about audio chaptering would be stronger with more datasets or stronger cross-domain validation.

There is little discussion of statistical significance, variance over seeds, or confidence intervals. Several comparisons, especially feature ablations and stratified/small-domain results, may not be robust enough to support fine-grained conclusions without uncertainty estimates.

The MLLM experiments are interesting but less controlled than the task-specific comparisons: they are restricted to shorter videos, depend heavily on instruction-following failures, and mix segmentation with transcription/title-generation constraints, making it hard to isolate multimodal reasoning ability from formatting and generation pathologies.

The paper would benefit from stronger fairness controls, such as text baselines using stronger transcript encoders or Whisper-derived representations, an audio-only model without ASR-pretrained encoders, and parameter/compute comparisons. Without these, the main empirical win is sound but its causal interpretation remains uncertain.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant and under-studied NLP/speech problem: chaptering long-form audio, where transcript-only framing is indeed limiting.

The evaluation-protocol discussion is useful. Distinguishing reference-transcript, ASR-transcript, hybrid alignment, discrete-time, and continuous-time protocols clarifies an important comparability problem in prior work.

The empirical scope is fairly broad: text baselines, acoustic feature augmentation, learned audio encoders, MLLMs, ASR-quality variants, duration/speaker stratification, and an AMI out-of-domain check.
The result that pauses substantially help transcript-based segmentation is plausible, well motivated, and supported by the ablation table.
The paper includes many implementation details in the appendix, including prompts, hyperparameters, feature extraction, and additional evaluation tables, which helps reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central claim that transcript-free audio segmentation is superior is overstated. The best AudioSeg model uses Whisper Large features, which likely encode substantial linguistic/ASR information and was trained on web audio similar to YouTube. This is not strong evidence that non-transcript audio alone outperforms text; it may be an implicit-transcript model with favorable pretraining/domain match.

The possibility of pretraining/data leakage or benchmark contamination is not discussed. Since YTSeg is drawn from YouTube and Whisper-style encoders are trained on large web audio corpora, this is a serious concern for claims about learned audio representations on YouTube chaptering.

Several methodological choices are underspecified or insufficiently justified: decision thresholds for boundary prediction, whether thresholds are tuned per model, variance over seeds, statistical significance, and calibration of predicted boundary counts are not clearly reported.

The evaluation protocol contribution is useful but not fully validated. T1 uses fixed 6-second bins and default segmentation metrics because this approximates average sentence length, but this choice can interact differently with native 6-second AudioSeg outputs versus text/MLLM outputs mapped through forced alignment.

The AMI generalization evidence is too small to carry much weight, especially for the <30 minute setting with only 4 test meetings. The task/domain also differs substantially from YouTube chaptering, so the conclusions about generality remain weak.

The MLLM experiments are exploratory and somewhat uneven: many systems are restricted to <30 minute videos, default inference settings are used, and failures in instruction following dominate. These results are informative but do not support strong conclusions about MLLMs for audio chaptering broadly.
Title-generation evaluation is secondary and not very convincing. Matching rates are low for some models, and automatic title metrics do not establish that the generated chapters are useful to users.

Reproducibility is only partial. The paper promises release of a toolkit and AudioSeg, but the manuscript itself does not provide enough detail on splits, thresholds, random seeds, variance, audio availability, and preprocessing decisions to make the strongest claims easily verifiable.

Overall, the paper contains useful empirical material, but its main narrative leans too heavily on results whose interpretation is confounded by pretrained ASR encoders, domain match, and evaluation-design choices. I would consider this borderline for Findings rather than main-conference acceptance.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and underexplored NLP/speech problem: chaptering long-form audio beyond transcript-only segmentation. The framing is clearly relevant to computational linguistics, especially speech-language interfaces, segmentation, summarization, and long-context document structure.

The evaluation protocol contribution is valuable. The distinction among reference-transcript, ASR-transcript, hybrid alignment, discrete-time, and continuous-time evaluation is careful, and the paper convincingly explains why transcript-space metrics can be lossy or misleading.

The empirical study is broad and informative: it compares text-only baselines, text plus handcrafted acoustic features, a transcript-free AudioSeg model, and multimodal LLMs; it further analyzes ASR quality, feature categories, duration, speaker composition, domain transfer, temporal grounding, and title quality.

The main result is practically interesting: AudioSeg with Whisper Large features substantially outperforms the best text-based systems on YTSeg under transcript-invariant time evaluation, supporting the claim that audio carries segmentation signal not captured by transcripts.
The ablations are useful. The pause-feature result, DeepFilterNet ablation, speaker-regime breakdown, and duration analysis all add interpretability rather than just reporting leaderboard numbers.

Reproducibility is reasonably supported by detailed prompts, hyperparameters, feature extraction descriptions, evaluation protocol definitions, and stated release of an evaluation toolkit and AudioSeg.
weaknesses: The strongest claim that transcript-free audio segmentation is superior is somewhat entangled with the use of Whisper Large as the best audio encoder. Whisper is trained for ASR and likely encodes linguistic content, and its YouTube/domain overlap may partly explain the gains; the paper acknowledges this but does not fully isolate acoustic versus latent textual information.

The core model contribution is moderate. AudioSeg is a sensible hierarchical architecture over frozen audio features, but it is not technically very novel; the paper’s main value is methodological and empirical rather than algorithmic.

Generalization evidence remains limited. YTSeg dominates the experiments, and AMI evaluation is small, with only 16 test meetings in the full setting and 4 in the <30 minute subset. This makes the cross-domain conclusions suggestive rather than definitive.

The MLLM evaluation is interesting but uneven: it is restricted to videos under 30 minutes for context reasons, uses mainly Qwen Omni models, and some comparisons are confounded by severe instruction-following failures, transcript omissions, and generation loops.

Some evaluation choices deserve more justification. The 6-second T1 grid is motivated by average sentence length, but metric sensitivity and boundary tolerance still affect rankings and absolute scores; the paper reports sensitivity analyses, but the choice remains partly task-conventional rather than validated against human utility.
The work would be stronger with statistical significance or confidence intervals, given the many close comparisons among text baselines, feature variants, and protocol settings.

The title-generation evaluation is less central and less convincing than the segmentation evaluation. ROUGE/BERTScore over chapter titles may not reliably measure usefulness, and matched-title evaluation depends heavily on boundary matching.

The release claims are encouraging, but the manuscript itself does not fully establish long-term reproducibility of data access, since YouTube-based audio/transcripts can be unstable or unavailable over time.
